newsitem.title: USA: U.S. scientists move toward safer prenatal tests.
newsitem.headline: U.S. scientists move toward safer prenatal tests.

text.p: A step toward a safer, simpler way of detecting genetic defects in a fetus based on a tablespoon-sized sample of the mother's blood was reported by U.S. scientists on Thursday.
The trial test was done on only two pregnant women and much more work was to be done before scientists know if the maternal blood screening will be effective and practical for widespread use.
The goal is to find a way of screening for defects early in a pregnancy, and without causing pain to the mother or danger to the fetus.

This approach can be used about 10 weeks into a pregnancy, and since it depends on identifying the few fetal cells that slip into the mother's bloodstream it does not involve invasive procedures into the uterus.

"I think if we can streamline the process, it could conceivably replace conventional testing methods ... We just need more experience," said Dr. Yet Wai Kan, of the University of California at San Francisco, whose study appears in the November edition of Nature Genetics.

In the two women studied, Kan was looking for sickle cell anemia, a blood disorder common among blacks, and beta thalassemia, a fatal form of anemia common among people of Mediterranean descent. Kan said the technique could also be applied for cystic fibrosis, Gaucher's disease and other genetic disorders.

The current methods of prenatal diagnosis -- amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling (CVS) -- are invasive and carry a one to two percent chance of causing a miscarriage. Amniocentesis results are not available until about the 20th week of pregnancy, and terminating a pregnancy at that point can be traumatic.

Several types of fetal blood cells can be detected in maternal blood, but not all are appropriate for genetic screening. For instance, one type can be found in the mother's blood for up to 27 years, so scientists would not know if the cells were from the current pregnancy or an earlier one.

In the study, Kan and his colleagues looked at cells known as erythroblasts, isolating them with a technique involving magnetic beads and magnets. They then had to scrape the fetal cells into a test tube and used a genetic amplification technique to analyze the DNA for mutations.
Both women's tests were negative and the results were confirmed by more conventional CVS testing.

"This is the first example of the accurate use of fetal cells in maternal blood for the non-invasive diagnosis of single gene disorders early in pregnancy," Bob Williamson, a scientist at the Murdoch Institute at Royal Children's Hospital in Parkville, Australia, wrote in an accompanying commentary in the journal.
